Can a rigid block be distinguished from a flexible block when the two complete
molecules have the same radius of gyration? Build a rod–coil diblock and compare
it with a size-matched Gaussian chain. This isolates a change in internal
structure from a change in overall size.

Start with the environment and linking workflow in the
[diblock tutorial](diblock-copolymer.qmd). All lengths below are in nm and q is
in inverse nm. `ThinRod` neglects the rod cross-section, so use it only where
that thickness is unresolved.

## Connect a rigid block to a flexible block

```text
rod.end1 ---- rod.end2 = coil.end1 ~~~~ coil.end2
```

The rod is rigid internally. The endpoint link allows the coil to orient
freely relative to it; this is not a model of a fixed-angle junction or a
wormlike chain.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pyseb

world = pyseb.World("RodCoilTutorial")
graph = world.Add("ThinRod", "rod")
world.Link("GaussianPolymer", "coil.end1", "rod.end2")
world.Add(graph, "rodCoil")
parameters = {
    "beta_rod": 1.0,
    "L_rod": 12.0,
    "beta_coil": 1.0,
    "Rg_coil": 3.0,
}
```

`beta` is the total excess scattering length of each block. Equal values give
the blocks equal scattering weight, even though their dimensions differ.

## Match the overall size and scattering length

Use the composite radius of gyration, which includes both internal block sizes
and their separation. With positive scattering weights this gives a useful
size-matched reference.

```{python}
rg2 = world.EvaluateRadiusOfGyration2("rodCoil", parameters)
world.Add("GaussianPolymer", "reference")
reference_parameters = {
    "beta_reference": parameters["beta_rod"] + parameters["beta_coil"],
    "Rg_reference": float(np.sqrt(rg2)),
}
print(f"Composite Rg = {np.sqrt(rg2):.4f} nm")
```

## Compare the scattering

```{python}
q = np.geomspace(1e-3, 3.0, 200)
rod_coil = np.asarray(world.EvaluateFormFactor("rodCoil", parameters, q.tolist()))
reference = np.asarray(world.EvaluateFormFactor(
    "reference", reference_parameters, q.tolist()
))
assert np.all(np.isfinite(rod_coil))
assert np.isclose(world.EvaluateFormFactor("rodCoil", parameters, 0.0), 1.0)

plt.loglog(q, rod_coil, label="rod–coil")
plt.loglog(q, reference, "--", label="size-matched Gaussian chain")
plt.xlabel(r"$q$ (nm$^{-1}$)")
plt.ylabel(r"$F(q)$")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```

Both curves have the same intercept and leading Guinier slope. At larger q,
the rod–coil model resolves a rigid block and a flexible block rather than one
Gaussian chain. Equal overall size alone does not determine the form factor.

```{python}
_ = pyseb.visualize(world, "rodCoil", parameters, height=440)
```

The viewer shows one seeded realization; the curve averages over coil
conformations and the relative orientations allowed by the link.

## Try changing the contrast

Keep the geometry fixed and reduce `beta_coil`. The normalized curve approaches
the isolated rod form factor as the coil becomes contrast matched. This changes
the scattering-weighted radius of gyration, so the reference above would need
to be matched again for a new size-controlled comparison.

```{python}
plt.loglog(q, rod_coil, label="both blocks visible")
for beta in (0.2, 0.0):
    changed = dict(parameters, beta_coil=beta)
    curve = world.EvaluateFormFactor("rodCoil", changed, q.tolist())
    plt.loglog(q, curve, label=f"coil beta = {beta:g}")
plt.xlabel(r"$q$ (nm$^{-1}$)")
plt.ylabel(r"$F(q)$")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```
